H ave you ever had conjunctivitis? If you have, you would understand that it is not a pleasant experience. This is bringing back some childhood memories. People would suggest different treatments. Looking back now, I can confidently say that those things were harmful to the eyes. Recently, one of my siblings, Mrs Temitayo Adefaye, who works in a hospital, told me about an outbreak of conjunctivitis popularly called “Apollo.” I had forgotten about our conversation until I saw a medical AI drama where a lady was in the hospital because she contracted conjunctivitis after using the same towel with her boyfriend who already had it. While we treat this as a medical emergency, let us also correct the erroneous belief that you can contract it by gazing into the eyes of a sufferer. The end-of-year breakout of conjunctivitis is driven by a combination of dry, dusty weather changes, increased transmission of cold and flu viruses and high volumes of holiday social gatherings. The most common infectious causes in adults are viral, whereas in children bacterial causes predominate. The viral infection may occur along with other symptoms of a common cold. Both viral and bacterial cases are easily spread among people. Viral conjunctivitis is frequently caused by adenoviruses, which are the same highly contagious viruses responsible for sore throats, colds and upper respiratory tract infections. When people cough, sneeze or blow their noses, respiratory droplets easily transfer to their hands. If they touch or rub their eyes afterwards, they introduce the virus directly into the conjunctiva. Let us see ways you can contract conjunctivitis: Respiratory droplets: Inhaling or coming into contact with airborne droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes near you. Direct contact: Touching or shaking hands with an infected person and then touching your own eyes. Indirect contact (fomites): Touching contaminated surfaces, objects or towels (where the virus can survive for days or weeks) and then rubbing your eyes. Since conjunctivitis is usually viral, antibiotic eye drops won’t help. Instead, the virus needs time to run its course. Viral conjunctivitis often begins in one eye and then infects the other eye within a few days. Your symptoms should gradually clear on their own. Antiviral medicines may be an option if your viral conjunctivitis is caused by the herpes simplex virus. What really is conjunctivitis? Conjunctivitis, also known as “pink eye,” is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin and clear layer that covers the white surface of the eye and the inner eyelid. It makes the eye appear pink or reddish. Pain, burning, scratchiness or itchiness may occur. The affected eye may have increased tears or be stuck shut in the morning. Swelling of the sclera may also occur. Itching is more common in cases that are due to allergies. Conjunctivitis can affect one or both eyes. In general, there are three main categories of pink eye: infectious, allergic and chemical. Infectious conjunctivitis Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Add us to your Preferred Sources Infectious pink eye comes in a few different types, including bacterial and viral. Bacterial pink eye is caused by staphylococcal or streptococcal bacteria. It typically occurs due to things like touching your eyes with unclean hands, sharing makeup, or having physical contact with someone who may also have conjunctivitis. Viral pink eye is usually caused by common cold viruses. It can occur if someone with an upper respiratory infection coughs or sneezes close to you. It can also occur when you have a cold virus yourself and blow your nose too hard. This can push the infection from your respiratory system to your eyes. Allergic conjunctivitis Most people with allergic pink eye have seasonal allergies. They can get pink eye if they come in contact with a substance, they are allergic to, like pollen. It is also possible to develop an allergic type of pink eye called giant papillary conjunctivitis if you wear hard contact lenses, or soft contact lenses that are not replaced frequently enough. Chemical conjunctivitis You can get this type of pink eye from irritants such as: chlorine in pools, air pollution, and exposure to other chemicals. Bacterial and viral pink eye are very contagious. For instance, if someone with viral pink eye touches their eye and then touches your hand and you touch your eyes, there is a chance you could get pink eye as well. Pink eye is typically contagious for as long as the person is having symptoms. The cause of conjunctivitis directly determines the treatment, as therapies that work for one type are completely ineffective or potentially harmful for another. Let us see the ways they are treated: The Nation’s editorial board member Omonijo dies at 63 NGE defends Obi’s conference participation, denies partisanship Kaduna begins free eye screening for 1,000 residents Chemical conjunctivitis Rinsing your eye with saline is one way to help ease symptoms if you are dealing with chemical pink eye. Topical steroids may also be prescribed if the case is severe enough. Bacterial conjunctivitis For a bacterial infection, antibiotics are the most common method of treatment. Adults usually prefer eye drops. For children, ointment might be a better choice because it is easier to apply. With the use of antibiotic medication, your symptoms will probably start to disappear in just a few days — but it is important to finish your entire prescription to lessen the risk of pink eye coming back. Viral conjunctivitis Most of the time, viral conjunctivitis is caused by the same viruses that cause the common cold. These cold viruses don’t currently have any treatments, but symptoms are usually mild and resolve on their own in seven to 10 days. In rare cases, other viruses like the herpes simplex or varicella-zoster virus can be involved, which can cause more serious infections. These viruses do have antiviral treatments, but these treatments can only be used for these specific types of viral infections. In the meantime, using a warm compress, or a cloth moistened with warm water, can help soothe your symptoms. Allergic conjunctivitis To treat pink eye caused by an allergen, your doctor will probably prescribe an antihistamine to stop the inflammation. Other treatments include antihistamine eye drops or anti-inflammatory eye drops. How can you prevent conjunctivitis? Practising good hygiene is one of the best ways to avoid and stop the transmission of conjunctivitis: Avoid touching your eyes with unwashed hands. Wash your hands often and thoroughly with soap and water. Only use clean tissues and towels to wipe your face and eyes. Try not to share cosmetics, especially eyeliner or mascara, with others. Wash pillowcases frequently. If you already have pink eye, you can help keep your friends and family safe by doing the following: Wash your hands regularly. Avoid sharing towels. Change your towel daily. Replace eye cosmetics after your infection clears. Follow your doctor’s advice on contact lens care. Take any medication your doctor has given you as prescribed. If your child has pink eye, it is a good idea to keep them out of school for at least 24 hours after they start treatment to keep them from transmitting pink eye to others. A study titled An Update on Viral Conjunctivitis Treatment Strategies: A Narrative Literature Review by Maheshver Shunmugam et al. concludes that while supportive therapy and hygiene measures remain central to care, antiseptic agents, specifically povidone–iodine, and topical steroids offer additional benefit in reducing symptom duration and complications.
